title: Understanding disaster risk where you live

say: Understanding disaster risk where you live.
This is the video for module one of Disaster Risk Management and Recovery.
Heavy rain is not a disaster. It is a hazard, an event that could cause harm.

panel.heading: Disasters are not just bad luck
items: A disaster is when people cannot cope
That depends on people and their situation

say: A hazard only becomes a disaster when it hits people and property that are exposed and not able to cope, so normal life breaks down.

say: Risk grows with hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and shrinks with capacity. Hazard: what has happened here before, and how often?

panel.heading: The four parts of disaster risk
items: Hazard: what has happened here before?
Exposure: is my home in its path?

say: Exposure: is my house, shop or farm in a low area, near a river bank or a drainage channel?

panel.heading: The four parts of disaster risk
items: Hazard: what has happened here before?
Exposure: is my home in its path?

say: Vulnerability: who in my house cannot move fast? Are my documents and savings easily destroyed?

panel.heading: The four parts of disaster risk
items: Hazard: what has happened here before?
Exposure: is my home in its path?

say: Capacity: do we have a plan, a kit, some cash and neighbours we can call?
You cannot stop the rain, but you can work on the other three.

say: For example, Amina and Grace live on the same low street. One night heavy rain floods it to knee height.

Amina keeps her stock on pallets and her papers in a zip bag on a high shelf. She has a plan and a torch. She switches off the mains while the floor is still dry, and the family is safe in 10 minutes.

left: Stock on pallets above the floor
Papers in a zip bag, high shelf
Safe at a neighbour's in 10 minutes
right: Stock in sacks on the floor

say: Grace keeps her stock and papers low, searches in the dark, and loses most of them.
The hazard was identical. The difference came from the parts a household can change.

say: The disaster management cycle has four stages. Mitigation lowers the risk itself, like clearing drains before the rains. Preparedness gets you ready, with a kit, a plan and drills.
Response is the hours and days during the event. Recovery is the weeks and months after, rebuilding stronger.
A drain cleared in April costs a few hours of work. A house flooded in September can cost years of savings.

Combine official forecasts with local memory. NiMet publishes a Seasonal Climate Prediction each year. NIHSA publishes an Annual Flood Outlook naming local government areas at risk. Check whether yours is listed.

items: NEMA, SEMA, LEMA: alerts and relief
Check the source before you share

say: NEMA coordinates response, with SEMA in each state and LEMA in many local governments. 112 is Nigeria's toll-free emergency number. Save it in your phone.

say: Fake flood alerts spread on WhatsApp every rainy season. Check the source before you forward one, because false alarms make people ignore real ones.

say: Give each hazard two scores from 1 to 5. Likelihood: how often it happens here. Impact: how badly it would hurt your household.

panel.heading: Likelihood x impact
items: Multiply for a score out of 25
Plan for the top hazard first

say: Multiply them. Halima lives about 400 metres from the Benue. River flood scores 4 times 5, which is 20. House fire scores 10. Windstorm scores 6.

panel.heading: Likelihood x impact
items: Multiply for a score out of 25
Plan for the top hazard first

say: So flood is her top priority, with fire safety second. A household truly ready for its main hazard is far safer than one that knows a little about everything.

panel.heading: Likelihood x impact
items: Multiply for a score out of 25
Plan for the top hazard first
panel.rule: Ready for your main hazard beats a little about everything.

say: An audit replaces the feeling of being somehow ready with facts. Check 20 items across five areas: water and food, light and communication, documents and money, health and safety, and people and plan.

panel.heading: Score your readiness out of 40
items: Add up the total out of 40

say: Health and safety includes a first aid kit, a sand bucket or extinguisher near the kitchen, and everyone knowing how to switch off gas and electricity. Score each item 2, 1 or 0.

panel.heading: Score your readiness out of 40
items: Add up the total out of 40

say: For example, Chioma's family scored 12 out of 40. 12 divided by 40, times 100, is 30 percent. Their weakest area was people and plan: no written plan at all.

panel.heading: Score your readiness out of 40
items: Add up the total out of 40

say: Sort every item that scored 0 or 1. Free and fast things, like writing numbers on paper, you do this week.

panel.heading: Sort every gap into three groups

cards.d: Write phone numbers on paper. Show everyone the gas valve. Do these this week.
A zip bag for documents, a torch. Schedule each one by date.
An emergency fund or a drill. Put them into your plan.

say: Low cost things, like a zip bag or a torch, you schedule by date.

say: Things that take time, like savings or a drill, go into your plan. And if children and elders cannot explain the plan, it is not yet real.

say: To remember. You cannot stop most hazards, but you can reduce exposure and vulnerability and build capacity.
Check outlooks and local memory, rank hazards, and audit your home out of 40.

say: Now practise. Map your four risk parts, interview elders and rank your hazards, and complete your baseline audit with two free fixes done within 7 days.
